clue.text: Harry turned up carrying a plant

indicators.note: the reversed word holds the next piece inside it, as if carrying it
in a down entry, turning a word up writes it from bottom to top, so it reads backwards

parts.note: to harry someone is to harass or worry them

explanation.surface: Someone called Harry arrives holding a potted plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' looks like a name but is the verb meaning worry; 'turned up' writes WORRY upwards as YRROW, and 'carrying' puts A inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Yarrow is a common flowering herb of meadows and verges, also called milfoil.

clue.text: Save? Get cross about worthless pieces here?

definitions.text: Save? Get cross about worthless pieces here?

indicators.note: the cross is placed round the back of the worthless pieces, coming after them

parts.note: save in the sense 'except' means bar, as in 'all bar one'
to get something is to gain it
base means low and worthless, as base metal
chessmen are pieces, so men
the letter T has the shape of a cross

explanation.surface: A shopper wonders whether to save money and gets annoyed at the junk on sale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' sends the cross, T, round behind BASE MEN. The whole clue doubles as a picture of the place: the cheap department of a store, full of low-value goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A bargain basement is the cut-price floor of a shop, where cheap or shoddy goods are sold.

clue.text: Said about Charlie: 'E's a know-all

indicators.note: the spoken word goes round the next letter, surrounding it

parts.note: oral means spoken, said aloud rather than written
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the 'E of 'E's is taken as the letter itself

explanation.surface: Someone in a Cockney voice says of Charlie that he thinks he knows everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts ORAL round C, giving ORACL; 'E's is the dropped-aitch Cockney 'he's', but only the E is used.
explanation.definitionFit: An oracle is a person thought to be an infallible source of wisdom, so a sage or know-all.

clue.text: Recalled mineral contained in seaweed

indicators.note: called back, so the word for the mineral is brought back from its end

parts.note: iron is a mineral nutrient and an ore metal

explanation.surface: A seaweed product is recalled because a mineral was found in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Nori is the dried edible seaweed used to wrap sushi in Japanese cooking.

clue.text: Fashionable but not after potential partner

parts.note: 'up to' a time means not after it, as in 'up to noon'
a date is someone you go out with who may become a partner

explanation.surface: A trendy person who is not chasing a potential partner.
explanation.definitionFit: Up to date means modern, current, following the latest fashion.

clue.text: Salt healthy, it's accepted?

indicators.note: the healthy word takes the next piece inside it, accepting it

parts.note: hale means healthy, as in 'hale and hearty'
it's is read as 'it is', so the word it

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether salt has been accepted as healthy after all.
explanation.definitionFit: Halite is the mineral name for rock salt, sodium chloride.

clue.text: Break under 50 Ronnie's last — it's unexpected

indicators.note: the letters come out in an unexpected order, so they are mixed up

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty

indicators.note: the last of Ronnie's letters is the one taken

parts.note: Ronnie's, the possessive, points at the name Ronnie
it's is read as 'it is', giving the word it

explanation.surface: A snooker break by Ronnie O'Sullivan stalls below fifty, a surprise for a player of his class.
explanation.walkthrough: The snooker picture makes 'Break' look like a run of pots, but it means a pause. 'unexpected' rearranges UNDER, L, E and IT.
explanation.definitionFit: An interlude is an interval or pause between parts of a performance or between events.

clue.text: Famous artist's space by town

parts.note: Tracey Emin is a British artist
an en is a printer's space, half an em
T is an abbreviation for town, as on maps

explanation.surface: A well-known artist's studio space next to a town.
explanation.walkthrough: Tracey Emin is a famous contemporary British artist, known for My Bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Eminent means distinguished and well known, standing out above others in a field.

clue.text: My visiting Paris disconcerted fliers

indicators.note: the exclamation calls in on the mixed-up city, going inside it
thrown into confusion, so the city name's letters are jumbled

parts.note: 'My!' and 'Cor!' are both exclamations of surprise

explanation.surface: A traveller's visit to Paris unsettled some airmen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks like a possessive but is an exclamation, the same as 'Cor!'; 'disconcerted' jumbles PARIS to AIRPS, and 'visiting' puts COR inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An air corps is a military flying service, so a body of airmen.

clue.text: Henry in literature showing signs of pain

indicators.note: the abbreviation sits in the word for literature

parts.note: writing is literature, written works
H is the abbreviation for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A Henry character in a novel is shown in agony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Henry' suggests a king or a novelist such as Henry James, but it is the physics unit, symbol H, placed 'in' WRITING.
explanation.definitionFit: Writhing is twisting and squirming, as a body does in agony.

clue.text: Parasite chief shortly about to leave

indicators.note: the shortened word goes around the next piece
cut short, so chief loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written
to go is to leave

explanation.surface: The head of a parasite group is about to depart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' makes CHIE, and 'about' puts GO inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The chigoe is a tropical flea, also called jigger, whose female burrows into the skin.

clue.text: Avoid where water's full of crap! Point taken — very reprehensible ultimately

indicators.note: the point is taken away from the sewer

parts.note: a sewer is the channel carrying foul water
E, east, is a point of the compass

indicators.note: at the end, so the last letter of reprehensible

parts.note: taken as written; its last letter is used

explanation.surface: An indignant complaint about filthy water, with a grudging admission that the point is made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point taken' reads as a phrase of agreement, but it drops an E from SEWER to leave SWER; 'ultimately' gives the E ending reprehensible.
explanation.definitionFit: To swerve is to veer aside so as to dodge something, so to avoid it.

clue.text: Ladies not finishing frivolous chatter? That's a hypothetical concept

indicators.note: silly, not serious, so the remaining letters are tossed about
without its finish, so the final letter goes

parts.note: taken as written
gas is idle chatter, as in 'a good gas'

explanation.surface: Ladies gossiping frivolously, ending in a remark about theory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not finishing' takes S off LADIES, and 'frivolous' turns LADIE into IDEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: An ideal gas is a theoretical gas whose particles have no volume or attraction, a model in physics.

clue.text: Overlapping signs for places of learning

indicators.note: the two signs overlap, so their shared letter is written once, not twice

parts.note: Libra and Aries are two signs of the zodiac, written one after the other

explanation.surface: Overlapping signs point the way to places of study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overlapping' means LIBRA and ARIES share the A where they meet, so one of the two A's in LIBRAARIES is dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Libraries are collections of books where people go to read and study.

clue.text: City game in shade

parts.note: EC is the postcode of the City of London
RU is rugby union

explanation.surface: A city game played in the shade.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district, whose postcodes begin EC.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecru is a pale greyish-yellow colour, the shade of unbleached linen.

clue.text: About time! A thorough search for where bodies are buried

parts.note: CA is circa, about
a comb is a thorough search, as in a fingertip comb of a field

explanation.surface: An exasperated 'About time!' as a thorough search for buried bodies finally happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About time!' reads as one exclamation but is two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A catacomb is an underground burial chamber, a tunnel of tombs.

clue.text: Bone's top piece put back

indicators.note: put backwards, so the joined pieces are read in reverse

parts.note: A1 means top quality, written AI in crosswords
a bit is a piece

explanation.surface: The top part of a bone is put back in place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top piece' looks like one phrase, but it is two pieces: AI (A1, first-rate) and BIT; 'put back' reverses AIBIT.
explanation.definitionFit: The tibia is the shinbone, the larger of the two bones of the lower leg.

clue.text: American comic's original lines — slick but not edgy material

indicators.note: origin, so the first letter of comic's

parts.note: taken as written; its first letter is used
RY is railway, the lines a train runs on

indicators.note: without its edges, so slick loses its first and last letters

parts.note: taken as written; its inner letters are used

explanation.surface: An American comedian's first routine is slick but has no edge.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrylic is a synthetic fibre used to make fabric, so a material.

clue.text: Complaint — coffee break about to be shortened

indicators.note: turned about, so those inner letters are read backwards
the phrase is cut short at both ends, leaving letters from inside it

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone moans that the coffee break is about to be cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be shortened' cuts 'coffee break' down to inner letters, FEEB from cofFEE Break; 'about' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A beef is a grievance or complaint, in informal speech.

clue.text: Article dissects southern French city and English town

indicators.note: the article cuts into the other pieces, sitting inside them

parts.note: Lens is a city in northern France
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A news article analyses a city in southern France and a town in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dissects' has the article cut into S plus LENS, a city in northern France. St Helens is a Merseyside town famous for rugby league and glassmaking.
explanation.definitionFit: St Helens is a town in north-west England, near Liverpool.

clue.text: Bring up smell in river

indicators.note: the smell sits in the river

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon
hum is British slang for a bad smell

explanation.surface: A bad smell rising from a river.
explanation.walkthrough: A hum is British slang for a stink; the Exe flows through Exeter in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhume is to dig up a buried body, bringing it up out of the ground.

clue.text: Trail suspect over bridge

indicators.note: doubtful, not to be trusted, so the letters are not in their proper order

parts.note: O is the cricket abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: Following a suspect's trail across a bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suspect' looks like a noun for a criminal but turns TRAIL into RIALT.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rialto is the famous bridge over the Grand Canal in Venice.

clue.text: These are found in Booker-winning novel

definitions.note: the answer is half of the novel's title, standing for the whole

indicators.note: the answer is found inside the run of letters in these clue words

parts.note: taken as written; the answer runs across these two words

explanation.surface: A reader remarks that certain words are found in a prize-winning book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found in' signals letters lying inside 'These are'. Iris Murdoch's 'The Sea, The Sea' won the Booker Prize in 1978; the answer is its title's repeated phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Iris Murdoch's 1978 Booker winner is titled by doubling this phrase, so the clue names that book loosely.

clue.text: Put the lid on drink

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to ... is to put a stop to, as in ... a rumour

explanation.walkthrough: 'Put the lid on' suggests sealing a bottle, but it means to quash.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to stamp out a rumour or plan and a whisky distilled in Scotland.

clue.text: Go round and round in flipping boring routine

indicators.note: flipped over, so the word is turned back to front
drilling into, so the ring goes inside the routine

parts.note: a rut is a dull routine
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A complaint about going round and round in a tedious routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' puts O inside RUT, giving RUOT; 'flipping' looks like a mild British swear word but reverses that to make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To tour is to travel around a place, visiting its sights.

clue.text: Literary tale-teller keeps home for fashion designer

indicators.note: holds the next piece inside

parts.note: the Miller tells a tale in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales
in means at home

explanation.surface: A literary storyteller keeps a house for a fashion designer.
explanation.walkthrough: The Miller's Tale is one of Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, so the Miller is the tale-teller who 'keeps' the word for home inside him.
explanation.definitionFit: A milliner designs and makes hats, a branch of fashion design.

clue.text: Ammo run out with day in battle

indicators.note: out of order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Soldiers run out of ammunition during a day of battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' mixes AMMO, RUN and D. Omdurman, near Khartoum in Sudan, was where Kitchener's army defeated the Mahdists in 1898.
explanation.definitionFit: The Battle of Omdurman in 1898 was a decisive British victory in Sudan.

clue.text: Nut — like to eat shells

indicators.note: encloses like a shell, so the eating word goes around the comparing word

parts.note: to chew is to eat
as means like, in comparisons

explanation.surface: A nut that you would eat shells and all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shells' looks like a noun for nut casings but is a verb: CHEW shells AS.
explanation.definitionFit: The cashew is a kidney-shaped nut from a tropical tree.
